title: Combustion of fuels
keyIdea: Hydrocarbon fuels burn by reacting with oxygen. With plenty of oxygen, combustion is complete: the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and the hydrogen becomes water, as in CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. With too little oxygen, combustion is incomplete: some carbon becomes carbon monoxide (CO) or soot (C) instead. CO is toxic, colourless and odourless, which is why homes with gas or oil appliances need CO alarms.
familyTip: Look at a gas hob or the pilot light on a boiler together: a healthy flame is blue. Ask what a lazy yellow or orange flame would mean, then find your carbon monoxide alarm and press its test button. Talk about why it has to be an alarm and not your nose that warns you.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: open a Bunsen air hole, balance methane, starve it of oxygen, watch CO take over blood cells, test the products.

kid: A fuel like methane is a hydrocarbon. It is made of only carbon and hydrogen. When it burns, it reacts with oxygen from the air. This gives out heat.

With plenty of oxygen, the burning is complete. Each carbon atom ends up in carbon dioxide, CO₂. Each pair of hydrogen atoms ends up in water, H₂O. For methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. A Bunsen burner with the air hole open burns like this, with a hot blue flame.

With too little oxygen, the burning is incomplete. There is not enough oxygen for every carbon. Some carbon makes carbon monoxide, CO, and some is left as soot, which is carbon, C. Water still forms. The flame turns yellow because hot soot glows.

Carbon monoxide is toxic. It has no colour and no smell. In your blood it sticks to the red blood cells much more strongly than oxygen, so less oxygen gets round your body. A faulty boiler or a blocked flue can fill a room with it, so homes need CO alarms.
adult: Ages 13 to 15. In England this is KS3 chemical reactions (combustion) and GCSE Chemistry (AQA 4.7.1.3 on the complete combustion of hydrocarbons and 4.9.3.1 on carbon monoxide and soot from incomplete combustion). Learners write word and balanced symbol equations, name the products of incomplete combustion and explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous.

Complete combustion: hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, for example CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O or C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Incomplete combustion happens when oxygen is limited: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O or CH₄ + O₂ → C + 2H₂O. It releases less energy, and the soot causes a yellow, luminous flame and blackened surfaces. Water can be shown by condensation on a cold surface and carbon dioxide by limewater turning milky.

Common mistakes: thinking less oxygen makes more carbon dioxide; listing hydrogen as a product; thinking a yellow flame is hotter; mixing up carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide; thinking CO can be smelled (the smell of mains gas is an added odorant, not CO); and balancing oxygen without counting the O in every water molecule. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen.

In the lab your child opens a Bunsen air hole and watches the flame and products change. They balance methane's equation atom by atom and give two methane molecules 4, 3 and then 2 oxygen molecules. They let CO from a blocked flue take the oxygen seats on red blood cells until an alarm sounds, then test the products of complete combustion.

practice.prompt: What are the products of the complete combustion of methane?
practice.hint: With plenty of oxygen, the carbon and the hydrogen each join oxygen.
practice.explain: The carbon becomes CO₂ and the hydrogen becomes H₂O: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

practice.prompt: An alkane has {n} carbon atoms and {=2*n+2} hydrogen atoms. When it burns completely, how many CO₂ molecules form from one molecule of it?
practice.hint: Every carbon atom ends up in its own CO₂ molecule.
practice.explain: {n} carbon atoms make {n} CO₂ molecules. The {=2*n+2} hydrogen atoms make {=n+1} H₂O molecules.

practice.prompt: An alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = {n} burns completely. How many H₂O molecules form from one molecule of it?
practice.hint: It has {=2*n+2} hydrogen atoms, and each H₂O holds 2 of them.

practice.prompt: A gas fire burns with a yellow, sooty flame. What does that tell you?
choices: It is short of oxygen: combustion is incomplete
It is burning hotter than a blue flame
practice.hint: What makes a flame glow yellow?
practice.explain: The yellow is glowing soot. Soot and carbon monoxide form when there is not enough oxygen, and the flame is cooler.

practice.prompt: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous?
choices: It has no colour or smell and stops blood carrying oxygen
It smells strongly and burns the lungs
It is only harmful as black soot
practice.hint: Think about the red blood cells in the lab.
practice.explain: CO binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, and you cannot see or smell it, so only an alarm can warn you.

pool.prompt: CH₄ + ?O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. What number balances the oxygen?
pool.hint: Count the oxygen atoms on the right: 2 in CO₂ and 1 in each H₂O.
pool.explain: The right has 2 + 2 = 4 oxygen atoms, so the left needs 2O₂.

pool.prompt: Which are products of incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
pool.hint: There is not enough oxygen for every carbon to become CO₂.
pool.explain: Some carbon forms CO and some is left as soot, C. The hydrogen still forms water.

pool.hint: Look for a product with only one oxygen on each carbon.
pool.explain: CO forms when oxygen is limited. The other two equations make only CO₂ and water.

pool.prompt: An alkane with {n} carbon atoms burns completely. How many CO₂ molecules form from 2 molecules of the alkane?
pool.hint: Each molecule gives one CO₂ for each carbon atom.
pool.explain: One molecule gives {n} CO₂, so two molecules give {=2*n} CO₂.

pool.prompt: Burning a fuel makes a gas that turns limewater milky. Which gas is it?
pool.hint: Limewater is the standard test for one product of complete combustion.
pool.explain: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Carbon monoxide does not.

pool.prompt: A boiler's flue is blocked. Why might the people in the house not notice the danger?
choices: Carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell
Carbon monoxide is only made outside
The gas smell would warn them about it
pool.hint: How do you notice most gases?
pool.explain: CO cannot be seen or smelled. The smell of mains gas is an added odorant, not CO, so a CO alarm is needed.

pool.prompt: Two molecules of an alkane with {n} carbon atoms burn completely. How many H₂O molecules form?
pool.hint: One molecule CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ has 2n + 2 hydrogen atoms, and each H₂O holds 2 of them.
pool.explain: One molecule has {=2*n+2} hydrogen atoms, which make {=n+1} H₂O. Two molecules make {=2*n+2} H₂O.

pool.prompt: Why does a Bunsen burner make a hotter flame with the air hole open?
choices: More oxygen lets the fuel burn completely, releasing more energy
The air hole lets soot escape so it glows brighter
pool.explain: Complete combustion turns all the carbon into CO₂ and releases more energy than incomplete combustion, so the blue flame is hotter.

pool.prompt: How does carbon monoxide harm the body?
choices: It binds to haemoglobin so blood carries less oxygen
It dissolves the lining of the lungs
It turns into soot inside the blood
pool.hint: Think about the oxygen seats on red blood cells.
pool.explain: CO binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, so less oxygen reaches the body's cells.
